about: The components of @acaprino/sigrid, written from its source by scripts/agents.mjs. `about` is the comment at the head of a file, `doc` the comment on a component. `props` are the props the toolkit declares; `passesOn` says the component also takes the props of the element or the part it draws. `types` are the object types those props are made of (a column, a notice, an option), with their fields. `also` are the other names the file exports: helpers, constants, types. `fromLibraries` are parts of Ark UI or Base UI the entry hands on unchanged.

files.about:
A theme from two colours (owner, 2026-11-22: «due colori e poi un accento»): the theme colour sets the buttons, the
selection, the links and the focus ring; the spot colour is the accent, the one loud colour, kept for the few things
that ask for attention now. The grays of the page are the third, quiet colour. The spot is not picked from the whole
wheel: three colours that go with the theme colour are proposed, from quiet to loud, and the engine then moves each
one until its contrast thresholds hold.

types.name: ColorThemePick
types.doc: What a colour theme is made from.

fields.name: color
fields.doc: The theme colour, `#rrggbb`.

fields.name: spot
fields.doc: The spot colour: one of the three proposals, or a colour of the user's own (`#rrggbb`). Absent: no spot.

files.about:
The eighteen free colors (for what the user colours: a folder, a group, a mark), in hue order (from red to pink). They are medium tints: the color is
user data, the same in both themes, so it holds up on both the light and the dark paper. An app that keeps the list
elsewhere too (on its server) keeps the same hex values there. A color that is already saved never falls out of the list.

components.name: ColorMatch
components.doc: Two colours for a theme: the theme colour, and the spot colour that goes with it. The spot is not picked from the whole wheel: three colours matched to the theme colour are proposed, from quiet to loud (`spotSuggestions`), besides none and one of the user's own. The sample below is drawn with the theme the two colours give (`colorTheme`).

props.name: colors
props.type: readonly { readonly color: string; readonly label: string; }[]
props.doc: The theme colours ready to pick, besides one of the user's own.

props.name: color
props.doc: The theme colour, `#rrggbb`.

props.name: spot
props.doc: The spot colour: one of the three proposals, a colour of the user's own, or none.

props.name: text
props.type: { color: string; spot: string; own: string; none: string; kinds: Record<SpotKind, string>; sample: { action: string; chosen: string; row: string; due: string; running: string; }; }

components.name: Dialog
components.doc: Modal window on a raised surface: a name to change, a profile, confirmations.

props.name: title
props.doc: Accessible title of the window.

props.name: footer
props.doc: Actions at the bottom (usually a primary `Button` and a `ghost` one).

props.name: restoreFocusTo
props.doc: Where focus goes when it closes: the window opens from state, not from a `Trigger` that would get focus back, and without this focus ends up on the `body`. `restoreFocusTo` is the element that opened it; `onCloseAutoFocus` speaks first and can decide for itself (`event.preventDefault()`, then move focus wherever it wants). Both are optional.

props.name: drawer
props.doc: The form opens in a side panel on the right, like a details sheet. Without it, it is a window in the center of the page: the short confirmations.

components.name: BaseColorChoice
components.doc: The base colour: the theme's own colours, one of the ready colours, or any colour. A colour makes the palette (`palette.ts`); `seed` is the colour a new palette starts from (the one on the page, so nothing jumps).

components.name: ChoiceCard
components.doc: An option: a small preview of what it does, its name and note, and the mark when chosen.

components.name: ChoiceCards
components.doc: The options of a choice as cards side by side: two per row on the phone, three (or two) on wider screens.

components.name: ChoiceGroup
components.doc: A choice with its label and, right below it, what it is for; the options follow. The label names the group for assistive technology (`aria-labelledby` on the options). Level 3 is a choice of the section, level 4 a part of one.

components.name: ChoicePreview
components.doc: The frame of a small preview inside an option: what choosing it looks like.

components.name: DensityChoice
components.doc: The density, among the ones the app offers (the toolkit's presets, `DENSITIES`, or its own definitions): each card draws three rows to scale. `chosen` is the id on the page; the app applies the one picked (`applyDensity`).

components.name: IconPackChoice
components.doc: The icon pack (R6): anchors for the eye beside the views, the groups and the settings.

components.name: PaletteComboChoice
components.doc: How the palette shares the page: each card shows the palette that combination makes from the base colour.

components.name: PaletteStrip
components.doc: A palette, not a miniature of the app (owner, 2026-11-20: «far vedere solo la palette e non tutto lo scheletro»): the page, the sidebar, the selection, the accent and the filled button, in the scheme of the pick.

components.name: ThemeCatalogChoice
components.doc: The app's ready-made themes, one card each with the theme's palette in the scheme shown. `chosen` is the id of the theme on the page, or null when a palette from a base colour replaces it (then none is chosen).

components.name: TonePresetChoice
components.doc: The tone, among three: each card shows that tone on the colours in use (the palette, or the theme).

components.name: TonePreview
components.doc: What a tone changes, side by side: the sidebar's tint and its selected row, four data colours and the filled button.

fields.name: theme
fields.doc: The first option: no palette, the theme's own colours.

types.name: ChoiceText
types.doc: A choice's name and, below it, what it is for.

fields.name: densities
fields.doc: Each density's name and note, by id. A density without words here shows its own label.

fields.name: notes
fields.doc: Below each theme's name, by id: what it is for.

fields.name: noEffect
fields.doc: Said in place of the three cards when the tone changes nothing: the colours in use have no hue (a gray theme), so the cards would be three copies of one preview. Absent: the cards are shown all the same.

components.name: PortalContainerProvider
components.doc: Where the overlays of this subtree mount: menus, popovers, selects, tooltips and dialogs. By default the page's `document.body`. An app that draws part of its React tree into another document (a popup window, an iframe) wraps that part with the other document's body, so its overlays open there and not in the page that owns the tree. `null` is the page's body: a provider whose element is not there yet (a layer that mounts with its children) keeps its place in the tree, so nothing under it is mounted twice when the element arrives.

components.name: ThemeGallery
components.doc: A compact theme picker. Each tile samples its own surfaces in the active scheme and tone. A null selection marks the optional custom tile, whose editor belongs to the caller.

SmoothUI (MIT) toast 4.0.0 — adapted for @acaprino/sigrid (https://smoothui.dev/r/base-nova/toast.json)
Park UI (MIT) toast 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/toast.ts)

From SmoothUI the surface of a notice is left: the dark card (the ink, with the paper as its text, as in the approved
preview), with the text, the action and the close button on one row, the quick choices on a second one. Park's
toast recipe is a light surface card: of it we take the form (l3 corners, the lg elevation, 16px of side padding, the
action in semibold) and the keys as outline keys, not its colors. Everything it does rests on Ark UI's Toast (`@ark-ui/react/toast`): a
toaster store, the `Toaster` region and one toast machine per notice (its time, its leaving). What Ark gives and what
stays ours:
- Ark: the region (F6 moves focus to it), the life of a notice (its timer, the "dismissing" phase that keeps it in
  the DOM while it leaves, `removeDelay`), the root and title parts, and the region as a branch of Ark's dismissable
  layers (a click on a notice is not "outside" an Ark popover).
- Ours: the list is the caller's (`items`); an effect carries it into the store (adds the new ones, closes the removed
  ones). The column: at most `COLUMN_MAX` notices one above the other, all readable, the newest at the bottom; a
  fourth pushes the oldest out from the top (Ark's `max` would keep the new one waiting instead) and the others move
  up one place. Ark's own layouts are not used (`overlap` off): its places follow its own list, which still holds a
  notice while it leaves, so the others would wait for it to be gone before closing the gap.
- the region is `role="status"` with `aria-relevant="additions"` and a name in English; a notice is not a `status`
  with `tabIndex=0` of its own: no extra Tab stop per notice;
- the time is Ark's, but it starts over: while the pointer is on the column or focus is inside it no notice counts
  down (`duration` Infinity), and when it is left each one is rearmed from the start;
- Esc does not close a notice on its own: only `durationMs` (which calls `onDismiss`), a fourth notice or the caller.
Motion: with `animated` the notices move with the list transition (`NOTICES` in `motion-impl`); without it, or with
prefers-reduced-motion, the same places are plain styles and nothing moves.

components.name: Toasts
components.doc: The notices: a column at the bottom right (in the middle on the phone), read by screen readers without interrupting. At most `max` (ten by default), one above the other, the newest at the bottom; one more pushes the oldest out from the top. With `durationMs` and `onDismiss` each notice shows the seconds left and a «×» to close it at once.

props.name: items
props.doc: The notices, oldest first. The column shows the `max` newest: one more pushes the oldest out (and calls `onDismiss`).

props.name: max
props.doc: How many the column holds, up to `COLUMN_MAX` (ten, R12 of the toolkit's rules, 2026-11-20).

props.name: inline
props.doc: In the page flow instead of fixed at the bottom: for documentation and previews.

props.name: durationMs
props.doc: After how many milliseconds a notice calls `onDismiss`. Without it (or without `onDismiss`) the notices stay until the caller removes them, as before. With the pointer on the column or focus inside it the time is suspended; when it is left the time starts over.

props.name: onDismiss
props.doc: Called once per notice when `durationMs` runs out, or when newer notices push it out of the column: the caller removes it from `items`.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The column moves: a notice enters and leaves, the others slide into place (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

types.name: ToastAction
types.doc: An extra action on a notice (a quick choice after a gesture): `pressed` marks it as already chosen.

fields.name: undo
fields.type: { label?: string; hint?: string | undefined; onClick: () => void; }
fields.doc: «Undo». `hint` is the key that does the same thing right now (for example «Z»): it is shown next to the button.

fields.name: actions
fields.doc: Quick choices, on a second row: groups of buttons (each group has a name for screen readers).

fields.name: kind
fields.doc: `error`: something failed and the user has to know. It never counts down (`durationMs` does not apply to it), it shows no seconds, and newer notices push the others out before it: it stays until it is closed (the «×», with `onDismiss`) or the caller removes it. A mark before the text says what it is, and screen readers hear «Error».

files.about:
The frame of an app: one layout with seven regions, after Imago's `im-shell`, so every app of the suite is laid out
alike and an app fills in only the regions it needs.

  ┌ title bar: app · views · toolbar · window buttons ───────┐
  ├ tabs: the views, when they are not in the bar ───────────┤
  ├ status: the last result · a summary ────────────────────┤
  │ sidebar │ content                    │ inspector         │
  │         ├ actions: the primary one at the end ───────────┤
  ├─────────┴ footer: service · counts · keys ───────────────┤
  └ bottom bar: the views, when they are at the foot ────────┘

The frame measures its own width, not the screen's, so a window half-snapped on a wide screen is laid out as the
narrow window it is. Three steps, Imago's:
- 1000px or more: the inspector is docked at the end and pushes the content; under it, it covers the end of the
  content as a panel with no backdrop (the page beside it keeps working);
- 850px or more: the sidebar is whole, or a rail if the user shrank it; from 620px to 850px it is the rail, whatever
  the user chose; under 620px it is out of the layout and opens as a drawer from a button of the title bar.
The steps are a recommendation, not a rule: an app with a narrower sidebar or a wider inspector passes its own
(`steps`), and a step set to 0 never happens (`steps={{ rail: 0, sidebar: 0 }}` keeps the sidebar whole at any width).
With `desktop` the frame is the window of a program and not a page (what Imago's windows do):
- its chrome is not selectable and keeps the arrow cursor, as in any program; the content, the body of the
  inspector, every field and whatever carries `data-selectable` stay selectable (theme.css);
- what opens over the window (dialogs, sheets, menus, the command palette) opens under the title bar and not over
  it, so the window can still be moved, minimized and closed while a dialog is open: the overlays of the frame mount
  into a layer that starts under the bar.
The keys and menus of the browser engine are a separate switch, `useDesktopGuard`, since a page in a tab keeps them.
Two forms, chosen with `frame`, with the same regions and steps:
- `line` (the default): one surface, the page, with a line between the regions;
- `sheet` (Xiox's frame, Imago's Smooth look without its glass): the title bar and the sidebar sit on the window's
  ground with no line and no fill of their own, and the work area (status, content, inspector, actions, footer) is
  one sheet of the page's surface with a line at its top and, where a sidebar lies beside it, at its start, with the
  large corner there. The ground is the sidebar's surface, so a light sidebar and the ground are one; a theme with a
  sidebar of its own colours (`data-sidebar="own"`, a dark or solid column) keeps its column on the lanes' surface.
  Where the sidebar is a drawer (under 620px) the sheet reaches the window's edge and has no corner.
The `Sidebar` and the `Inspector` read the step from the frame (`useAppShell`), so the app passes them as they are.
Without a way to measure (a server, a test) the frame is the wide one.

props.name: titleBar
props.doc: The bar at the top (a `TitleBar`).

props.name: tabs
props.doc: Directly under the bar, across the whole window: the views of the app (a `Toolbar` of `ToolbarTabs`), when they are not in the bar.

props.name: status
props.doc: Under the bar: the last result and a summary, one line.

props.name: sidebar
props.doc: The navigation (a `Sidebar`).

props.name: inspector
props.doc: The details of what is selected (an `Inspector`).

props.name: actions
props.doc: Under the content: the actions on it, the primary one last (R3: one).

props.name: footer
props.doc: The foot: the state of the service, counts, the keys that work now.

props.name: bottomBar
props.doc: Under everything, across the whole window: the views of the app as tabs at the foot (a `Toolbar` of `ToolbarTabs` with `edge="top"`).

props.name: desktop
props.doc: The frame is the window of a program: chrome that is not selectable, and overlays that open under the title bar. Leave it off for a page in a browser tab.

props.name: frame
props.doc: `line` (the default): one surface with lines between the regions. `sheet`: the title bar and the sidebar on the window's ground, the work area one sheet with a corner, as in Xiox.

props.name: steps
props.doc: The app's own steps, all or some, in place of the recommended ones (`APP_SHELL_STEPS`); 0 switches a step off.

props.name: contentLabel
props.doc: The name of the content for screen readers, and where the skip link goes.

props.name: children
props.doc: The content: what the app is for. It scrolls by itself.

components.name: Inspector
components.doc: The details or the form of what is selected, at the end of the frame. It is not modal: the rest of the window keeps working beside it. Docked it is a column with a line at its inner edge (R4); in a frame under 1000px it is a raised panel over the end of the content. Closed, the content takes its room.

props.name: title
props.doc: What it shows («Details»): its heading and its name for screen readers.

props.name: onOpenChange
props.doc: With it, a button in the heading closes the inspector; as a drawer, Esc does too.

props.name: footer
props.doc: Under the body, always in sight: the actions on what is selected.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The drawer slides in (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

fields.name: sidebar
fields.doc: `full`: the user's choice holds. `rail`: forced to its icons. `drawer`: out of the layout, opened over the page.

fields.name: inspector
fields.doc: `docked` beside the content, or a `drawer` over its end.

Park UI (MIT) avatar 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/avatar.ts)
From Park's `avatar` recipe comes the form (its subtle variant, its full shape): a round tile with the picture
cropped to fill it, or the initials in medium weight when there is no picture. Ours: three sizes on the toolkit's
control heights (36, 32 and 28px at normal density; Park's go from 24 to 64px), 12px initials below the largest, and a
neutral fill for every person: the quiet gray of the label pills, with the ink. A person's colour is not a fill
(R10: data colours are dots); an app that gives people a colour puts a dot beside the name.
Behaviour: Ark UI's Avatar, which shows the initials until the picture has loaded and again if it fails.
The name is the avatar's accessible name, unless `decorative` says the name is written beside it.

props.name: name
props.doc: The person's name: the accessible name, and the source of the initials.

props.name: src
props.doc: The picture. Without one, or while it loads, or if it fails: the initials.

props.name: decorative
props.doc: The name is written beside the avatar: hide it from screen readers.

props.name: color
props.doc: An identity fill, `#rrggbb`, for an app whose people or accounts are told apart by colour (a mail app's accounts). The initials take the ink with the better contrast on it (white or black). Without it the tile is the neutral one (R10: a colour for a person is a dot, not a fill): this is for what the app chose on purpose.

props.name: children
props.doc: Drawn in place of the initials (an icon for «all accounts»); the picture still wins when it loads.

SmoothUI (MIT) badge 4.0.0 — adapted for @acaprino/sigrid (https://smoothui.dev/r/base-nova/badge.json)
Park UI (MIT) badge 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/badge.ts)
From Park's `badge` recipe comes the form (its md size: 20px tall, 12px medium text, 8px of side padding, l2 corners,
tabular numbers) and the variants under our names: `default` is its solid, `secondary` its subtle, `outline` its
outline, all in the neutral gray (R2: labels never take the accent; R5: a badge is for a label, never a count).
Icons are 14px (R7).
From SmoothUI's Badge we keep the plain `<span>` with `data-slot` and `data-variant` and the 12 px icons. Our variants stay (with the tokens from `theme.css`, not SmoothUI's colors) and so does `asChild`, here with
Base UI's `useRender` instead of Radix's Slot. Removed: `size`, the success/warning variants and `StatusDot` with its
looping pulse (nobody uses them; no looping motion in the toolkit). The badge does not animate.

SmoothUI (MIT) smooth-button 4.0.0 — adapted for @acaprino/sigrid (https://smoothui.dev/r/base-nova/smooth-button.json)
Park UI (MIT) button 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/button.ts)
From SmoothButton we keep: the plain `<button>` with `type="button"` by default and `asChild` without Radix's Slot
(here with Base UI's `useRender`, which merges classes, styles, handlers and ref like the Slot). Our variant and size
names stay (the ones the package uses).
From Park's `button` recipe comes the form: l2 corners, and its variants and sizes under our names. The label is
medium (Park's is semibold: lighter here).
Variants: `default` is Park's solid, `secondary` its subtle in the neutral gray, `outline` its outline (with the 3:1
control border), `ghost` its plain, `destructive` its subtle in red; `link` is ours. A neutral subtle chip is
`QUIET_CHIP` below, for an app's chips: it is not a public variant.
Sizes: `default`, `sm` and `xs` are 36, 32 and 28px at normal density, one 4px step under Park's md, sm and xs (40, 36
and 32px, which is the large density); `lg` is the default height with a 16px label; the `icon-*` sizes are the same
heights, square. Colors are the theme engine's
tokens, not Park's palettes. Focus: the toolkit's ring (`lib/focus.ts`, R8).
The variant `secondary` is Park's subtle in the neutral gray (R4: no border and shadow together).
Motion, only with `animated` true and without prefers-reduced-motion: the button goes down a little while pressed
(`tapScale`) and, if asked, grows under the pointer (`hoverScale`). The gestures are attached to the `<button>` that is
already there (`pressable` in `motion-impl`), so the element is the same with animations on or off and nothing
remounts when the Motion chunk arrives. With `animated` false the DOM is the same as before.
Park's `loading` state, without its spinner (the owner's decision of 2026-11-20: no looping animation, as the
attachment viewer): a busy button keeps its size and its place, is `aria-busy` and `aria-disabled` (it keeps focus,
unlike `disabled`), ignores clicks and the pointer, and may show the caller's `loadingText` ("Saving…") in place of
its label. With `loadingText` the label and the loading text share one grid cell, so the width is the wider of the
two before, during and after the wait.

props.name: asChild
props.doc: Renders the child in place of the `<button>` (for a link that looks like a button).

props.name: animated
props.doc: The button goes down a little while pressed (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

props.name: hoverScale
props.doc: Scale under the pointer, with `animated`. Default 1: still.

props.name: tapScale
props.doc: Override the default press scale (0.96 with at most 2px of travel per edge).

props.name: loading
props.doc: Waiting for the result of its action: the button keeps its size, is `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-disabled="true"`, keeps focus and ignores clicks. No spinner and no looping animation.

props.name: loadingText
props.doc: The label while `loading` ("Saving…"), written by the caller. The button reserves the room of the wider of the two texts, so it does not change size when the wait starts or ends. Absent: the label stays.

Park UI (MIT) date-picker 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/date-picker.ts)

From Park's `date-picker` recipe (and its component, which draws each day as a plain icon button) comes the look: the
title between two plain arrows, the weekday row in semibold muted text, the days as 36px plain buttons (Park's sm)
with l2 corners and a quiet fill under the pointer, the chosen day solid in the accent (Park's solid variant), today
marked by a short accent dash under the number, 16px of padding. The grid itself is not written here: it is the day,
month and year views of Ark UI's DatePicker (`@ark-ui/react/date-picker`). It lives inside a `DatePicker.Root` (see
`internal/date-field.tsx`), which holds the value.
Ark gives the grid and its keyboard (arrows between days, PageUp and PageDown for the month, with Shift for the year,
Home and End for the week, Enter chooses; one day only has `tabIndex` 0), the days outside the month, today, the
title that opens the months and then the years, and the announcement of the month when it changes.
Ours: the sizes (`--cell-size` is the density token `--control-sm`, 2.25rem at `normal`, 2.75rem with a finger; the days outside the month softer), the names in English (see `CALENDAR_WORDS`), a real `<button>` for each day (Space
chooses too), the weekday headers left readable by screen readers, with the full name in `abbr`, and Home and End
for the start and the end of the week, as in the APG date grid (Ark's go to the start and the end of the month).

props.name: onPressSelected
props.doc: A click, Enter or Space on the day that is already chosen calls this instead of choosing it again (the reminder uses it to remove the day).

SmoothUI (MIT) checkbox 4.0.0 — adapted for @acaprino/sigrid (https://smoothui.dev/r/base-nova/checkbox.json)
Park UI (MIT) checkbox 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/checkbox.ts)
From Park's `checkbox` recipe comes the form of the control (its sm size: an 18px box with l1 corners, its solid
variant: when checked the box is a fill with the mark in the contrast color). The border at rest stays our `input`
token (3:1, WCAG 1.4.11): Park's is its hairline `border`. The fill is the accent, with the label colour the engine
pairs with it for the mark (the owner's design of 2026-11-22; it was the ink). An app may round its own boxes in its own CSS, through the shape token `--radius-check`.
From SmoothUI's Checkbox we keep: Base UI's Root rendered as a real `<button type="button">` (`nativeButton`,
so a `<label htmlFor>` labels it and Space checks it; Enter does not, per WAI-ARIA), the Indicator with the stroked
check mark and the dash for the indeterminate state. Our API stays (the one from before: `checked` and `defaultChecked`
also accept "indeterminate", `onCheckedChange` receives `boolean | "indeterminate"`, `data-state` on the control), the
tokens from `theme.css` and the enlarged touch area. Removed: SmoothUI's automatic animations (AnimatePresence, spring,
`pathLength`, exit): with `animated` the mark grows once, with the Web animation from `motion-impl` (`popCheck`),
only after the user's click, never on a mark already present at mount and never with `prefers-reduced-motion`.

props.name: checked
props.doc: Checked (controlled). "indeterminate" shows the dash; a click moves it to `true`.

props.name: defaultChecked
props.doc: Initial state when uncontrolled.

props.name: onCheckedChange
props.doc: Called with the new state when the user checks or unchecks.

props.name: animated
props.doc: The mark appears with a short animation when the user checks (off by default, never with prefers-reduced-motion).

Park UI (MIT) combobox 102769c — recipe translated to Tailwind for @acaprino/sigrid (https://github.com/chakra-ui/park-ui/blob/102769c/packages/preset/src/recipes/combobox.ts)
From Park's `combobox` recipe comes the form (its md size, its outline variant): the field is the toolkit's input
(40px, l2 corners, the 3:1 border) with the chevron at its end, and the list is the select's (l2 corners, the md
elevation, 4px of padding, a 2px gap, rows at least 40px tall with 8px of side padding and l1 corners). The row
under the pointer or the arrows is the quiet fill; the chosen one carries a check, in the ink (Park's is its accent).
Behaviour: Ark UI's Combobox: typing filters, the arrows move, Enter chooses, Esc closes the list first. The text
must end as one of the options: on leaving, a text that is none goes back to the chosen one.
Ours: the options are filtered here by their label, ignoring case, unless the caller answers `onQuery` with a new
list (people from a server); the list is not moved to a portal (as the date field's card: it stays inside the sheet

row has a title and, if the app has them, a second line under it, something before the title (an avatar, an icon), a
short fact at the end (a date, a size) and whatever else the caller adds there (a `Count`, a label).
It speaks the one language of every list of the toolkit:
- the row the user chose has the selection tint, stronger text and a short accent bar at its start (R1), and under
  the pointer a row takes a share of that tint;
- a row not read yet has a dot in the accent before its title and the title in semibold (R2: unread is one of the
  accent's places); the dot's slot stays when empty, so the titles line up;
- a row is one line as tall as the density's row, or two lines; with a finger it is at least 44px.
A row is a button, or a link with `href`, so nothing in it is a control: a button cannot hold a button.

How far a task is: a bar (`Progress`), a ring (`ProgressRing`) or blocks (`ProgressSegments`), one API for the three.
Written by hand: Ark's Progress names the bar with its own value («45%») and gives no `aria-valuetext`, and there is no
keyboard to inherit; here the app names the bar, the toolkit says the value. The form is Park UI's progress recipe
(102769c): a track 8px (`sm`) or 10px (`md`) tall with the corners of a control (l1), the range filling it from the
start. Not taken from it: the stripes, the gradient of its indeterminate state and its animation (no gradient, no
loop but the skeletons: DESIGN.md), and the pill shape (round only for avatars, dots and switches, R7).
The ring and the blocks are ours; Park's circular recipe was not read.
The colours: the track is the quiet fill (the ink at 6%), the range is the accent as progress (R2); done is the
success colour and a failure the destructive one, each with a word (DESIGN.md "Status": a colour is never alone).
Nothing moves: the range jumps to the value, as the steps do. A progress that changes by events (an upload) is not a
gesture, so no tween (DESIGN.md Motion). The range is `primary`, the fill of the accent, as in the checkbox and the
switch (DESIGN.md Colors).

For screen readers: `role="progressbar"` named by the app, with `aria-valuenow` and, always, `aria-valuetext` («45%»,
«Complete»). The visible text repeats it and is hidden from them. A page that updates a value often should
announce the end and the failure only, in a live region of its own, not every percent.

The steps of a task as a path (a signup, an import, a lesson): numbered dots joined by a line, that light up one by one
as the user goes. It shows what is done, where the user is and what is left, and the next step by its name: people
finish when they know what remains. The accent is progress (R2): a step done is a check on the accent tint, the step
the user is on is the one solid dot, the steps to come are a quiet fill with their number, and the line is the accent
as far as the steps done. Round, as a dot may be (R7). Nothing moves: the state is always on the screen, which
is what an ADHD eye needs. Steps done can be buttons that go back to them (`onStepSelect`), never the ones to come.
For screen readers it is an ordered list; the step the user is on has `aria-current="step"`, and each step says whether it
is done, current or not started (`words.steps`, in any language).

A table: rows of the same things, each with the same facts in columns. These are the parts of its form and nothing
more: a `<table>` in a box that scrolls, a heading row, rows and cells, drawn with the toolkit's tokens so every
table of an app reads as the others do.
- A row is as tall as the density's row (44px with a finger), with a line under it and no other frame (R4).
- A heading is small muted text (the label size); a column of numbers is set at the end, in tabular figures (R5).
- The row chosen has the selection tint, stronger text and a short accent bar at its start (R1), as in every list;
  under the pointer a row takes a share of that tint.
What a table does (sorting, filtering, choosing columns, drawing only the rows in sight) is not here: `DataTable`
(the `./table` entry of the package) does the first and the last on TanStack Table, and an app with a table of its
own drives it with the library it likes and draws it with these parts.

The bar at the top of a window: the place of its name and of its toolbar, on the same row as the buttons that
minimize, maximize and close it. It is plain web: on a page in a browser it is the app's top bar and nothing else.
What makes it the frame of a window is given from outside, so the toolkit knows no window API:
- the empty parts of the bar move the window. The standard way is the `app-region` property, set in theme.css on the
  bar and taken off every control inside it; a host that marks its drag regions with an attribute of its own gets it
  through `dragProps`, which the bar, the toolbar inside it, its title and its spacers all carry (such a mark often
  counts only on the element under the pointer);
- the room the system keeps for its own buttons over the page (the window-controls overlay of an installed web app)
  is left free: theme.css reads it into `--titlebar-start` and `--titlebar-end`, and an app can set the two itself;
- where the system draws no buttons, `WindowControls` draws them and calls the app back; the app talks to its host.
  On Windows 11 a host can lay the system's own hit area over the maximize button, so the Snap Layouts open from it:
  the pointer then never reaches the page's button. `maximizeRef` gives the host the button to measure, and
  `maximizeState` shows on it the hover and the press the system reports (Imago's window does this).
The bar is as tall as a dense control and 8px above and below it (`--titlebar-height`), on the page's own surface
with a line under it (R4: a line, no shadow). With `size="compact"` it is the thin caption of a classic desktop
program: the smallest control and 2px above and below it (32px at normal density), and the toolbar inside it takes
the small size by itself. Nothing else changes: it is a measure, chosen with a parameter.

The last one takes the accent under the pointer, as in Imago: closing a window destroys nothing, and red is kept for danger. They only call back: what minimizes, maximizes and closes the window is the app's.

props.doc: Each button is drawn only if its action is given.

props.doc: The middle button, for a host that needs its rectangle.

props.doc: The pointer over the middle button as the system sees it, when the system and not the page receives it.

The toolbar: one row of actions that is a single Tab stop. Base UI's `Toolbar` carries the behaviour (the arrows
move among the items, Home and End reach the ends, a disabled item stays reachable); the form is the toolkit's
`Button` recipe at the dense height, so an item is the same control as everywhere else.
- `ToolbarButton` is an action. With no children it is an icon alone: its `label` is its accessible name and the
  hint under the pointer (with the `shortcut` after it, as plain text: R5). With children it is an icon and a word.
  `pressed` makes it a switch (a filter that is on, a panel that is open): the selection tint, never the accent fill.
  One item of a toolbar may be `variant="default"`, the one solid action of the screen (R3); the rest stay quiet.
- `ToolbarSearch` is a search box that takes no room until it is asked for: a magnifier that opens into the
  toolkit's `SearchField` on a press (or when the app opens it from its own key), and closes again with Esc, or when
  it is left empty. While it holds text it stays open, so what filters the page is always in sight.
- `ToolbarBrand` is the app at the start of the bar, as in Imago's apps: a small square in the accent holding the
  initial of the product's name, and the name beside it, or the name alone (`mark={false}`). With `page` the place
  follows the name after a chevron («Daodan › Settings»). No drawn logo: the hue and the name tell the apps apart.
- `ToolbarTabs` are the views of the app as words in the bar, after the brand, as in Xiox («Cleanup · Registry ·
  Developers · Settings»): the view the user is in has the stronger text and a short bar in the accent under it. The
  same tabs can sit in a toolbar of their own directly under the title bar (`AppShell`'s `tabs`), in a bar at the
  foot of the window (`bottomBar`, with `edge="top"` and, on a narrow window, `layout="stacked"`: the icon over the
  word), or small in the status bar (`size="sm"` in the `footer`).
- A button with a word shows its `shortcut` after the word, as plain text («Commands Ctrl K»): the way into the
  command palette.
- `ToolbarSeparator`, `ToolbarGroup`, `ToolbarTitle` and `ToolbarSpacer` lay the row out. Inside a `TitleBar` the
  root, the title and the spacers also carry the bar's drag attributes, so the empty parts of the bar move the window.
Short of room the bar gives way in fixed steps, measured on the toolbar itself and not on the screen (a container
query, as Imago's frame does: a window half-snapped is narrow on a wide screen). Under 448px a button with an icon
and a word keeps the icon alone, and the search shown as a field is its magnifier; under 256px the title goes.
What the user needs to act (the buttons) is never what gives way.
Two sizes, chosen with a parameter: `md`, and `sm` for the dense bars of a classic desktop program (28px items, a
20px mark). A toolbar in a compact `TitleBar` is `sm` by itself. Text buttons that open a `DropdownMenu` («File»,
«Edit», «View») make the menu bar of such a program out of the same parts.
Icons are the app's (an `Icon`, or any 16px drawing); the magnifier is functional chrome, as in `SearchField`.

From Park's `tooltip` recipe comes the form: a solid ink card with l2 corners, the sm elevation, 12px semibold text,
8px by 6px of padding.
From SmoothUI we keep the primitive (Base UI's `Tooltip`: Root, Trigger with `render`, Portal, Positioner, Popup) and the
shape of the card (ink on paper, small text). Adapted to icon-only buttons: the text is the button's accessible
name (`label`, the same as its `aria-label`), not free content; no Provider (each
hint has its own delay, 500 ms), no controlled state. Removed: SmoothUI's CSS transitions
(the opacity and transform transition with the entrance scale): with `animated` true (off by default, never with
prefers-reduced-motion) the card fades in a few pixels from its button in 100 ms (`enterTooltip` in `motion-impl`).
Base UI places and labels it.
The hint does not capture the pointer (`pointer-events-none`, `disableHoverablePopup`), closes on click on the
button and with Esc, and sits below sheets and windows (`z-[45]`: above the drawer, z-40, below the sheets, z-50). The accessible
name stays only the `aria-label`: the card is `aria-hidden` (Base UI does not add `aria-describedby`), so a
screen reader does not hear it twice.

A theme from two colours, and the accents that go with a base colour (owner, 2026-11-22: «due colori: la base, che
di suo è il bianco ma si può cambiare, portata sulle tonalità chiarissime, e un accento scelto con i principi della
colorimetria, suggerito in automatico»).
- The base is the page. Whatever colour is chosen, only its hue stays: it is brought to a very light tone (an OKLCH
  lightness of 0.985 and a chroma of 0.018 at most), so the page is a white with a breath of that colour and the text
  keeps its contrast. No base, or a gray one, is the neutral white. In dark the same hue is a very dark tone.
- The accent is what the eye is led by (R2). It is not picked from the whole wheel: from the base's hue the classical
  harmonies give the hues that go with it, all on one wheel, OKLCH's, where equal turns are equal steps for the eye:
  the split complement (150° to either side), the complement (180°), the triad (120°), the neighbours (30°) and the
  base's own hue. Each is drawn at the lightness and saturation of a button, inside what a screen can show.
- They are ranked. A split complement comes first: it is clearly another colour without the vibration of the exact
  opposite. A hue that would read as the red of an error is moved out of its room and ranked lower, and one beside
  the green of success or the amber of a warning loses a little: an accent must never be taken for a status. A hue
  between yellow and lime loses more: yellow is itself only when it is light, and at the lightness a button needs
  under its label it turns to olive.
A white or gray base has no hue to start from: the proposals are then eight hues spread round the wheel, the blue
first. The theme engine then moves every colour until its contrast thresholds hold, as for any theme.

The icon packs (R6 of the toolkit's rules, 2026-11-20): icons are visual anchors for the eye, and the user picks the
pack in Settings. A component asks for an icon by what it means (`settings`, `delete`), never by a pack's own name:
the pack in context draws it. Lucide is the default (line, the toolkit's stroke). Two packs take the colour of the
theme: Phosphor Duotone and Solar Duotone, drawn in the text colour with a lighter second tone. Three are in their
own colours: Fluent Color, Fluent Emoji Flat and Twemoji, drawn emoji that look the same on every device (the
device's own emoji font left the packs on 2026-11-21: the owner did not like it). The drawn packs are not npm
dependencies: their drawings are in `icon-packs.generated.ts`, written by `scripts/icon-packs.mjs`. Functional
chrome (chevrons, ×, the search magnifier) stays Lucide.

From Park's `tags-input` recipe (md) comes the look: the field 40px tall with l2 corners and 6px of side padding,
6px between the chips, each chip 28px tall with l1 corners and its own 20px remove button. What the field does rests
on Ark UI's TagsInput (`@ark-ui/react/tags-input`).
Ark gives: Enter and the comma that close a label, a pasted «a, b, c» split into labels, the text left in the box
added when the field is left, the arrows that walk the chips from the box (Delete or Backspace removes the one
reached), the remove button of each chip with its name, the announcements to screen readers, one Tab stop for the
whole field. Ours: the chip is the neutral `Badge` with a dot in the color of its name (`tag-color.ts`, R10); the words are about
«labels», in English; a label already there is not added again whatever its case; Backspace in the empty box removes
the last label at once (Ark would first select it and remove it at the second press); a chip is not edited in place;
a comma that arrives with other text in one go (an autocorrection, a keyboard's suggestion) closes the labels before
it and leaves the rest in the box (Ark would add the text it had before that event).
With `suggestions` the box is also a combobox (Ark UI's Combobox, on the same text box): while the user writes, the
labels that match and are not in the field yet are listed under it; the arrows move, Enter or a click adds the one
reached, Esc closes the list only. Any other text is still a label of its own (Enter, the comma, leaving the box).
No animation.

What makes a page behave as the window of a program and not as a page in a browser. An app that runs in a window of
its own (no address bar, no browser around it) calls `useDesktopGuard()` once; in a browser tab it does not.
- The keys a browser engine keeps for itself do nothing: reload, print, find, history, the page's source, the
  developer tools, back and forward (with Ctrl, or with Command on a Mac). They are refused in the capture phase and not stopped, so the app's own handler
  for the same key (Ctrl+F for its search, Ctrl+S in its editor) still runs.
- The engine's own menu on a right press is refused, except where it is useful: in a field (it offers editing) and
  over selected text (Copy). An app's own context menu is not touched: it shows its own.
- The back and forward buttons of a mouse do not navigate.
- A picture or a link is not dragged out of the window, unless the app made it draggable.
`ownKeysIn` names the places that run their own keys and menus (a terminal, a code editor): there nothing is refused.
The technique is the one Imago's windows use (its `guardDesktop`); this is the toolkit's own writing of it. The
native side of the same guard (navigation limited to the app's origin, new windows refused) is the app's host.

A zone that takes a file: dropped on it, or chosen with the system picker, so dragging is never the only way (WCAG
2.5.7). The look is the attachments zone's (Park's `file-upload` recipe): the raised sheet with l3 corners and a 2px
dashed border in the control colour that turns solid ink while a file is dragged over it (the accent is not for this,
R2), two lines of text and no upload icon (the words say it, R6), 96px tall so it is an easy target with a mouse and a
finger. Ark UI's FileUpload gives the real button that opens the picker, the input behind it (outside the
accessibility tree and the tab order, emptied before each choice so the same file can be chosen again) and the checks
of type, size and count; the drop is the toolkit's `useDropTarget` (a drag that starts in the page is left alone).
The words are the app's: the label (the button's name, the same while dragging or busy), the hint (its description),
the line while dragging and while busy, and the error under the zone. Busy, the button keeps its focus and ignores
clicks and drops, like a loading Button. No animation.

Palettes from one base colour (owner, 2026-11-20: "selezionando un colore di base deve in automatico creare una
palette complementare + accento, e far scegliere solo tra 3 combinazioni"). Material Color Utilities finds the hues
that go with the colour (its complement by temperature, its tertiary); the theme engine then builds the theme from
them, so every contrast threshold holds as for the catalogue's themes. Two mood colours set the theme, the accent
makes it the user's.

types.name: PalettePick
types.doc: The user's palette: one base colour (`#rrggbb`) and how the rest follows from it.

files.about:
The shape of a theme definition, and the fonts. The toolkit ships no themes: each app passes its own definitions
and the engine (theme-engine.ts) derives every colour from them, guaranteeing the contrast
thresholds. Four things make a theme: the tint of the grays (`hue`) and how strong it is (`chroma`), the accent
(saturation and hue) and the sidebar: `tenue` (light, the tone of the app's ground), `scura` (a near-black, almost
neutral column in both schemes) or `piena` (in the theme's colour, with the selected item solid). Optional: a strong
`fill`, a `second` colour for the selection, or a curated palette's own `surfaces`.

fields.name: accent

fields.name: second
fields.doc: A second color (OKLCH chroma and hue) for the selected item, when it is not the accent's: the page and the selection are one calm color, the filled button another that stands out ("teal to focus, orange to act").

fields.name: spot
fields.doc: The spot color (`#rrggbb`): a second, louder color for the few things that ask for attention now (what is due, what is running), never for structure. Without it the spot tokens are the theme's own fill and accent.

fields.type: { readonly light: Surfaces; readonly dark: Surfaces; }
fields.doc: A curated palette: the theme's own surfaces, ink and accents in each scheme, as `#rrggbb`, instead of the common lightness ladder. The engine still corrects text, accents and borders until they hold the contrast thresholds.

types.name: ThemeRadii
types.doc: The corner radii of a theme in px (`ThemeDef.radii`).

files.about:
The theme engine: a theme from the catalog (theme-catalog.ts), in light or in dark, gives the values of all the `--color-*`
tokens and of the shape variables. The starting lightness values are those of the approved sketch
(design/bozzetti/lista-attivita.html, `coloriDi`), the same for every theme: that is why every theme reads the same. The colors
are computed in OKLCH, brought back to sRGB by reducing chroma, and the contrast is guaranteed in the computation, on the final
hex values: a color below the threshold is darkened on light backgrounds and lightened on dark ones until
it gets there. Fixed, never from the theme: the destructive red, the ink of the icons on the user's colors.
The solid button (`primary`) is the accent as a fill: in light it coincides with the accent as text, in dark it is a
solid and deeper tone of the accent with light text, while the accent as text (`accent`) stays light.
A theme with a strong accent (`fill` in the catalog) has a fill of its own, vivid, in both schemes: its label is the
light or the dark one, whichever reads better on it, and the accent as text stays a separate, readable tone.

fields.name: tint
fields.doc: The strength of a derived tint (`match`, `complement`). Default: medium.

fields.name: second

files.about:
The words of the toolkit. A component's content is the app's: what a field holds, what a button says, the title
of a dialog all come from the caller. What is left here are the few words a component has to say by itself: the
name of a close button, the announcement of a label added, «Page 2 of 5». They are placeholders, in English: an app
replaces them, all or some, once for the whole tree with `WordsProvider`, in the user's language, and again when
the language changes. A word that takes a value is a function, so each language orders and inflects it as it needs.
Where a component also takes the word as a prop (`placeholder`, `clearLabel`, `textNotice`), the prop wins.
The helpers that return a sentence outside a component (`kindLabel`, `stateText`, `overLimitNotice`, `withinLimit`)
take the words as their last argument: `useWords()` gives them to an app's own component.

the columns and the sorting, `@tanstack/react-virtual` for the rows in sight: npm dependencies, pinned, see
THIRD_PARTY.md); the form is the toolkit's `Table` parts. It lives in its own entry of the package (`./table`), so
an app without a table does not load either library.
- A column says its heading, what a cell shows, and the value it sorts by. Without that value the heading is a
  word and not a button. A press sorts up, a second down, a third puts the rows back as they were given. The
  heading says how it is sorted with `aria-sort`, and with an arrow for the eye.
- With `onRowPress` a row is pressed with the pointer or with Enter and Space; the arrows, Home and End move among
  the rows, which are one Tab stop, as in a list: the row that had the focus last, or the chosen one, or the first
  in sight. A press on a control inside a cell (a button, a link, a field) is that control's and not the row's.
  The chosen row (`current`) has the selection tint (R1).
- With `virtual` the box needs a height (`className="h-96"`): the rows outside it are not in the page, two spacer
  rows keep the scrollbar honest, and each row is measured as it is drawn, so any density and a finger's 44px hold.
  Home and End go to the first and the last row of the data. A row scrolled far out of sight is no longer in the
  page, and the focus it had goes with it: Tab comes back to a row in sight.
- `columns` is best made once (outside the component, or with `useMemo`): a new array at every paint sorts the
  rows again at every paint.
An app that needs more of a table (filters, pinned columns, groups) drives TanStack Table itself and draws it with
`Table`, `TableRow` and `TableCell`: this component is the common case, not a wall around the library.

files.about:
A long list of which only the rows in sight are in the page: ten thousand messages cost what thirty do. The rows
are the toolkit's own (`ItemRow`, or any `<li>`); this part is the box that scrolls and the choice of which rows to
draw, on TanStack Virtual (`@tanstack/react-virtual`, an npm dependency, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md). It has its own
entry of the package (`./virtual`), so an app with short lists does not load the library.
- The rows of a list are all as tall as each other, so one of them is measured as it is drawn and the rest follow:
  any density holds, and so do the 44px of a finger. `estimateSize` is only where the first paint starts from.
- The room of the rows not drawn is kept as padding, so the scrollbar is the one of the whole list.
- For screen readers it is a list that says how many items it holds and where each one is (`aria-setsize`,
  `aria-posinset`): what is not drawn is still counted.
The box needs a height (`className="h-96"`, or a place in a column that gives it one).

props.doc: How many rows are drawn beyond the ones in sight, on each side. Default 8.

props.doc: Classes of the box that scrolls: its height.

files.about:
A list the user puts in order: each row has a handle that moves it, with the pointer, a finger or the keyboard. The
behaviour is dnd-kit's (`@dnd-kit/core` and `@dnd-kit/sortable`, npm dependencies, pinned: THIRD_PARTY.md); the form
is the toolkit's. It has its own entry of the package (`./reorder`), so an app with no such list does not load it.
- The handle is the only thing that drags: the rest of the row keeps its presses, its fields and its text.
  With the keyboard: Space takes the row, the arrows move it, Space puts it down, Escape puts it back. Screen
  readers hear where it is at each step, in the app's words (`words.reorder`). While a row is taken, Escape is
  the list's: a dialog or a sheet the list is in stays open.
- The row taken is raised on the sheet colour with the `float` elevation and no border (R4), and follows the pointer
  up and down only. The others make room for it: at once, or sliding in 200ms where the app has motion on
  (`animated`, or `MotionProvider`), never with reduced motion.
- The list is the app's: `onReorder` gives the new order and the app keeps it. Nothing is kept here.

props.doc: What tells an item from the others.

props.doc: The name of an item: of its handle («Move Inbox»), and what screen readers hear while it moves.

props.doc: What a row shows beside its handle.

files.about:
A field for text with a little form: bold, italic and underlined words, two kinds of list, a quote. The editing is
TipTap's (`@tiptap/react` and its starter kit, on ProseMirror: npm dependencies, pinned, see THIRD_PARTY.md); the
form is the toolkit's: the border and the focus ring of a field, and above the text the toolkit's own `Toolbar`
with the icons of the pack the user chose (R6). It has its own entry of the package (`./rich-text`): TipTap is the
heaviest thing the toolkit rests on, and an app that writes no formatted text does not load it.
- What the row of buttons offers is all the field does: headings, code, links and rules are switched off, so a
  paste or a shortcut cannot bring in what the user has no button to take away. The value holds what was written
  and nothing else: no empty paragraph is kept after a list (Enter twice leaves a list or a quote).
- A button that is on (the caret is in bold text) says so with the selection tint, as any switch of a toolbar.
- The value is HTML, the app's to keep: `onChange` gives it at every change. A value that comes from outside (a
  draft opened) replaces the text and is not a step of the undo: Ctrl+Z never brings the other draft back. The
  field's own changes never loop back, also when the app hands them back late (a store, a round trip): a value
  the field itself gave a moment ago is not taken for a new one.
- It takes what a `FormField` gives its control (`id`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, `required`). A `<label>`
  names only the browser's own fields, so the text finds the label that points at its `id`, takes its name from it
  (`aria-labelledby`) and takes the focus when the label is pressed, as an input does.
- Text is 16px below 860px, so a phone does not zoom, and 14px above.

props.doc: The text, as HTML.

props.name: aria-label
props.doc: The name of the field for screen readers, where no label names it.

props.name: required
props.doc: Said to screen readers; whether an empty text is accepted is the app's to check.

props.doc: The text cannot be changed: half opacity, no buttons.

props.name: className
props.doc: Classes of the box around the buttons and the text: the least height of the text is its own (`min-h-24`).

files.about:
A canvas for a graph of things and what joins them (tasks and what they wait for, the parts of a project, notes
that lead to other notes): the user moves over it, looks at one thing and what is joined to it, opens and closes
what hangs from a thing and, where the app lets them, draws: adds a thing, joins two, takes one away. The canvas,
its pan and zoom, the lines and the joining by hand are React Flow's (`@xyflow/react`), the places of the things
are dagre's (`@dagrejs/dagre`): npm dependencies, pinned, see THIRD_PARTY.md. The form is the toolkit's. It has its
own entry of the package (`./graph`) and its own stylesheet (`./graph.css`), so an app without a graph loads neither.
- The graph is laid out by itself, in ranks: from the start to the end of the line (`direction="right"`) or from
  the head to the foot (`"down"`). The user does not place things by hand, so nothing can be lost off the canvas.
- A thing is a raised surface with a shadow and no border (R4): an icon or a dot of its colour (R10), a name, a
  line under it. The chosen one has the selection tint (R1); what is joined to it stays as it is and the rest is
  dimmed, so the eye finds the neighbourhood. The app shows the details of the chosen thing where it likes (the
  `Inspector` of the frame).
- A thing with others hanging from it has an arrow: closed, it says how many it hides, and the graph is laid out
  again without them. What can be reached another way stays in sight.
- The keyboard is the one of a tree, and the things are one Tab stop: Down and Up go through what is in sight,
  Right opens or goes to the first thing that hangs, Left closes or goes back to what it hangs from, Home and End
  reach the ends, Enter chooses. With `editable`, Delete takes the thing away. Screen readers hear a tree: the name
  of a thing, its level, whether it is open, how many it hides.
- With `search` a field finds things by name; the others are dimmed, and Enter goes to the first one found,
  opening what hides it.
- With `editable` a thing shows its handles: drag from one to another thing to join them, press the plus on the
  chosen thing to hang a new one from it. Every change is asked of the app with `onChange`, which keeps the graph
  (and its undo, R12): nothing is kept here but what is open and where the view is.
The cost is the layout, done again when the graph changes or a thing opens or closes: about 30ms for 200 things in
sight, 200ms for a thousand, most of a second for three thousand (measured). A larger graph starts with its
branches closed (`defaultCollapsed`). Moving the view costs little: only what is in it is drawn.
Nothing moves by itself: the layout jumps to its new places, with or without animations. The name of React Flow
stays at the foot of the canvas, as its makers ask of whoever does not pay for it.
